claims.text: Formation of a stable, multi-component oxide scale during wear governs the wear performance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings.
The oxide scale provides a protective barrier that reduces metal-to-metal contact.
The oxide scale limits plastic deformation during sliding wear.
Exposure to a moderate oxygen partial pressure at elevated temperature will promote oxide formation relative to an inert-atmosphere baseline.
Oxidation kinetics are significant between room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures under the proposed conditions.
Controlled oxidation produces a multi-component oxide layer on the coating surface.
The oxide layer modifies the distribution of stress during sliding.
Reduced direct contact and plastic deformation mitigate material loss and enhance wear resistance.
Oxidizing conditions will produce lower wear rates than the inert-atmosphere baseline.
Oxidizing conditions will produce a lower coefficient of friction than the inert-atmosphere baseline.
A continuous and adherent oxide scale will be present after testing under oxidizing conditions but absent or less developed after inert-atmosphere testing.
An inert atmosphere permits minimal oxidation and consequently produces less-protective surface layers and higher wear rates.

The proposed mechanism should operate when temperature and oxygen partial pressure sustain oxide-scale formation without deleterious substrate oxidation or complete degradation of the alloy microstructure.
Extremely high temperatures or oxygen pressures can cause rapid, uncontrolled oxidation and fall outside the proposed regime.
